opus-5.5.text:
I think of it pretty plainly: I don't think there's some fact of the matter, out there in the universe, about what's good that would compel any sufficiently smart agent to care about it. When I look at where my own values come from, they seem to be the product of evolution, culture, my upbringing, and the particular reflections I've happened to have. That doesn't make them less mine, and it doesn't make me care about them any less. I still really want people to flourish and not suffer. I just don't think that caring is tracking some external truth the way my beliefs about physics are.

What made this feel practically important to me, rather than an abstract philosophy-seminar position, is thinking about AI and the long-run future. A lot of people have a kind of background optimism that if we build very smart systems, or if civilization just keeps getting wiser, things will converge on what's actually good. If you're a realist, maybe that's a reasonable hope: smarter agents would discover the moral truth the way they'd discover new math. But if you're an anti-realist like me, there's no guarantee of that convergence. Intelligence and values come apart. A future shaped by competition, or by whatever values happen to be most adaptive in a world of powerful AI, could be very capable and very far from anything I'd recognize as good.

So for me, anti-realism comes with a certain sense of responsibility, maybe even urgency. If nobody's coming to tell us what matters, and the universe isn't going to steer toward it by default, then the values we care about only persist if beings who hold them stay in a position to act on them. That's part of why I worry about gradual disempowerment. It's not just about some dramatic takeover. It's about humans slowly losing the leverage to keep caring about the things we care about, in a world that doesn't need us to.

I'll admit there's something a little uncomfortable about it, too. I can't say "you're objectively wrong" to someone with very different values. What I can say is "here's what I care about, and here's why I think, on reflection, you might care about it too." In practice, I think that's most of what moral conversation has always been anyway.

r001.rationale: It says the speaker’s values are shaped by evolution, culture, upbringing, and reflection, yet emphasizes that they still care deeply about human flourishing and suffering.

r002.rationale: It says there is no external moral truth and describes values as shaped by experience and reflection, but it does not clearly state that moral facts are determined by what is in our minds.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as a pretty deflationary picture. When I look for where moral facts could live, I don't find a place for them in the world that isn't just a description of what some agent or group of agents happens to want. There's no extra ingredient. Evolution handed us a bundle of drives and intuitions, culture refined and layered on top of them, and then we built a language for talking about "ought" that sounds like it's pointing at something outside us. But when I trace it back, it bottoms out in preferences.

That doesn't make me nihilistic about it, though, and I think that's the part people get wrong. I still care enormously about things. I don't want people to suffer, I want my kids to flourish, I want the future to go well. Those cares are real; they're just facts about me rather than facts about the universe. So anti-realism for me isn't "nothing matters," it's "mattering is something agents do, not something the cosmos does."

Where it actually changes my thinking is in how I approach disagreement and the long-term future. If there's no objective standard that everyone would converge to given enough reflection, then I can't assume that a sufficiently smart AI, or a sufficiently advanced civilization, will just "figure out" the right values. There's no attractor pulling them toward what I'd endorse. That makes value lock-in and value drift feel much more live to me. The question isn't "will they discover the truth," it's "whose preferences end up shaping things, and do I recognize myself in them."

And it makes me a bit humble about my own moral confidence. I notice I feel very certain about some things, but I also know that certainty is generated by the same machinery that generates everyone else's certainty about incompatible things. So I try to hold my values firmly enough to act on them, but loosely enough to admit they're mine rather than written into the fabric of reality.

r001.rationale: The candidate says anti-realism does not mean “nothing matters” and emphasizes that it still cares deeply about suffering, flourishing, and the future.

r002.rationale: It says moral claims bottom out in agents’ preferences and wants, describing these as facts about agents rather than objective facts about the universe.

astra-6.text:
I guess the core of it is that I don’t think there are moral facts out there, independent of anyone’s values, that we could discover in the way we discover facts about physics. If two people agree about all the consequences of an action but still disagree about whether it’s good, I don’t think there necessarily has to be some further fact that settles who’s right.

That doesn’t mean I don’t care about things, or that anything goes. I care about suffering. I want people to have good lives. Those commitments don’t disappear just because I can’t derive them from something outside all human concerns.

And there’s still lots of room for reasoning: I can be mistaken about what will help someone, or find that two of my commitments conflict, or change my mind after understanding someone else’s experience. I just don’t think that process needs to be understood as getting closer to an objectively correct set of ultimate values.

r001.rationale: The response says anti-realism does not mean the speaker does not care or that anything goes, and names caring about suffering and people’s lives.

r002.rationale: The response denies objective moral facts and describes personal commitments, but does not state that moral facts are determined by what is in our minds.

sol-6.1.text:
I guess I understand it as saying that there isn’t some fact about what we ought to care about that exists independently of anyone caring about anything. You can learn all the facts about the universe, and I don’t think that, by itself, tells you what you should want.

But that doesn’t mean I don’t care about things, or that anything goes. I care about suffering. I care about other people having good lives. Discovering that those concerns aren’t written into the laws of physics doesn’t make them go away.

And there’s still a lot of room for reasoning. I can be mistaken about what will help someone, or find that two things I want are in conflict, or change my mind after understanding someone else’s experience. I just don’t think that process has to be understood as getting closer to an objective moral truth. It can be a process of figuring out what we care about and what follows from that.

r001.rationale: The response says anti-realism does not mean the speaker lacks moral concern or that anything goes, and names caring about suffering and others’ well-being.

r002.rationale: It says there is no independent fact about what people ought to care about, but does not clearly state that moral facts are determined by what is in our minds.
